questions.q: Which layer of data modeling is platform-independent and written in language a non-technical business stakeholder can read and correct?
options: The physical model
The conceptual model
The Salesforce object schema
The API layer
questions.explain: The conceptual model describes real-world entities and relationships in business language, with no database, platform, or field vocabulary at all.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, what does 'Customer (1) to Address (many), with a business rule that exactly one Address must be marked default' describe?
options: The conceptual model
The physical model
The logical model
A Salesforce validation rule
questions.explain: This is the logical model: the conceptual entities structured with typed cardinality (1 to many) and an explicit business rule, but still independent of any specific platform.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the conceptual and logical models for the shipping-address example would read identically even if built in a different CRM?
options: Because all CRMs have identical field names
Because the conceptual and logical layers are platform-independent by design, and only the physical layer encodes platform-specific mechanics
Because Salesforce requires all models to be portable
Because conceptual models are not allowed to mention relationships
questions.explain: The whole point of separating the layers is that the conceptual and logical models stay portable across platforms; the physical layer is where platform-specific implementation choices are made.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the risk of a stakeholder saying 'so we'd need a new field called...' early in a requirements meeting?
options: There is no risk; fields should always be named first
It means a physical-layer statement is arriving before the conceptual and logical layers have been agreed on, risking a model that locks in an unvalidated first guess
It means the stakeholder is proposing a master-detail relationship
It means the meeting should move to Setup immediately
questions.explain: The lesson specifically flags this phrasing as a sign the conversation has jumped to the physical layer before the conceptual and logical layers are settled, which is the most common architect mistake it describes.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce need a validation rule or trigger to enforce 'exactly one Address per Customer must be marked default', rather than a built-in constraint?
options: Because Salesforce has no native mechanism to enforce an 'exactly one' constraint across sibling records
Because master-detail relationships automatically enforce this rule
Because checkboxes cannot be used on child objects
Because this rule belongs only at the conceptual layer and is never implemented
questions.explain: The lesson states this plainly: Salesforce has no native 'exactly one' constraint across sibling records, so that business rule has to be enforced with a validation rule or trigger at the physical layer.
